item.title: Gayle King stunned after learning dissenting Clancy trial juror was a Black man
item.description: Co-host Gayle King was visibly stunned on "CBS Mornings" after learning the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial was reportedly a Black man.
item.content:encoded:
"CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King was stunned after learning that the lone dissenting juror in the Lindsay Clancy trial was purportedly a Black man during a Friday interview.

Paula Devlin, one of the jurors who was part of the 11-person majority in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible for strangling her three young children, explained that the lone holdout was a Black man and the only person of color on the jury in an interview with King on the network morning show.

"Whoa. I have to sit with that for just a second," said King, who appeared visibly flustered by the revelation.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR WHO BACKED THE DEFENSE ALSO PUBLICLY CHEERED KAREN READ'S ACQUITTAL

Devlin also said ages among the jurors ranged between 22 and "70-ish."

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial last week after jurors could not agree on a verdict. They told the court they were split 11-1, with the lone male holdout being the only one voting to convict Clancy of first-degree murder for the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan.

A fellow juror, Nick Dargie, 25, told ABC News that the lone holdout juror at one point attempted to mimic the way Clancy killed her three kids with an exercise band and water bottle.

"He took the exercise band out of the bag, grabbed an empty water bottle and tied the band around the water bottle and pulled it," Dargie said. "I was just so shocked that he did that."

"I was shocked, it didn't make any sense to me. Like, we're not in here to play detective or it's not a game of Clue. Like, this is serious. I asked him why," he added.

LINDSAY CLANCY JURY RECAP: DAY 5 ENDS WITH NO VERDICT AFTER RARE INSTRUCTION

Dargie said the holdout juror refused to explain how witness testimony helped prove his stance.

"There was several times I would ask him to show us evidence or, you know, describe a witness testimony that helped to prove what he was saying, and ... he couldn't," Dargie said. "There wasn't a single piece of evidence or witness testimony that he used to prove why he was thinking the way he was, which is why we ultimately sent in that note."

Dargie was referring to the note sent by the jury foreperson, who reported that one juror was refusing to follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt.

Curtis Houck, the Managing Editor of the NewsBusters division of the Media Research Center, a media watchdog group, helped the clip go viral by sharing it in a social media post and summarizing the exchange.

He later spoke to Fox News Digital about the clip, arguing the host's surprise was one of many responses from media figures that speak volumes about American culture.

"The woke women propping up these 11 jurors and either directly or indirectly smearing this holdout juror have had their lives completely upended by this stunning declaration. King — whose best friend Oprah recently taped a sympathetic, pro-Clancy special — came off as though she had just been hit by a proverbial bus, meaning she clearly thought he was a White male she could stereotype," he said. 

"The fact that she further pressed for information about his age showed the dangers this holdout juror is facing, now that he has been identified by gender, race, and a rough age," Houck added. "King will now be known by many for this cartoonish reaction."

Fox News’ Adam Sabes and Michael Ruiz contributed to this report.

item.title: Mark Wahlberg, Martha Stewart and more mark 25 years since 9/11 with emotional tributes
item.description: Mark Wahlberg, Martha Stewart and Hugh Jackman lead Hollywood's emotional tributes marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Hollywood is pausing to remember.

As America marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the nation is coming together for ceremonies and moments of silence honoring the 2,977 people killed.

Across Hollywood, celebrities are sharing personal reflections, tributes and messages of remembrance on the anniversary of the day that forever changed America.

PETE DAVIDSON SAYS BECOMING A DAD CHANGED HOW HE VIEWS FATHER'S DEATH ON 9/11

Mark Wahlberg shared a video on Instagram showing an American flag raised on a flagpole and waving in the wind, captioning his post, "This anniversary is always a gut punch of emotions…words just can’t say it all. #neverforget911 #freedomisntfree "

Martha Stewart offered a particularly personal remembrance, recalling where she was when she watched the attacks unfold on television while in Tokyo.

"In 2001 I was in Tokyo when we saw on television live footage of the destruction of the WorldTrade Center towers. Of course we could not reach the United States for hours and could not find out the fate of our family members and friends. We stayed glued to the television for news and we tried to figure out how we could get back to the United States. We decided to take the train to Kyoto where we knew we could find peace and beauty amidst the horror of the day."

ROB RIGGLE RECALLS 'APOCALYPTIC' SCENE AT GROUND ZERO WHILE SEARCHING FOR SURVIVORS AFTER 9/11

Stewart went on to describe finding an unexpected moment of solace at a temple in Miho, Japan, after a friend encouraged her group to visit.

"She was stranded in Paris but urged us to go to the temple at Miho for solace and rest. We drove through the entrance tunnel, past the museum (both designed by IM Pei) and onto the huge beautiful temple (photo one). It had been designed by the very same Minoru Yamasaki who was the architect of the World Trade Center !!!!"

"As we entered the deserted temple (it was closed that day) the organ played America the Beautiful for us. All of us in my small group stood in awe and disbelief and we all cried for the people lost that day in the attack that changed America forever!"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Dean Cain shared a personal tribute on X alongside a selfie. An American flag was visible in the background, along with a shelf displaying a small cross and other decorative items.

"Never Forget. The cross behind my desk is made from steel from the fallen towers," he wrote.

Hugh Jackman shared a video montage on his Instagram Story that included a black-and-white photo showing the immediate aftermath at Ground Zero following the Sept. 11 attacks in New York City, with the words, "REMEMBER," while encouraging followers to "Show up for one another @911memorial."

Sarah Jessica Parker also honored the anniversary, sharing a video montage of New York as a beam of light rose into the night sky behind One World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan. 

"September 11th, 2026, 25 years. We never forget. I ❤️ NY. Forever. And ever. X, SJ," she wrote.

The British royal family also marked the anniversary on X, highlighting a commemorative Changing of the Guard ceremony at Buckingham Palace.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Remembering all those affected by the tragic events of 9/11, 25 years ago today," the post read.

The ceremony included performances of both the U.S. and U.K. national anthems, as well as "Hymn to the Fallen" and "Amazing Grace." 

The royal family also noted that King Charles III and Queen Camilla paid their respects at the 9/11 Memorial in New York earlier this year during their state visit to the United States.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The anniversary will also be marked in New York City through music.

Cyndi Lauper is set to perform alongside previously announced artists Lainey Wilson and John Ondrasik of Five For Fighting during "9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan."

The performances will honor the nearly 3,000 people killed in the attacks, as well as the survivors, families, first responders and communities whose lives were forever changed.

item.title: New York Times accused of framing Muslims as true victims of 9/11 in anniversary coverage
item.description: The New York Times faced accusations of framing Muslim Americans as the true victims of 9/11, but the paper calls the criticism "disingenuous."
item.content:encoded:
The New York Times on Friday was accused of treating Muslims as the true victims of the terror attacks of September 11, 2021, but the paper insists any criticism is a "disingenuous" attempt to stoke outrage.

"The Times can't remember 9/11 without bemoaning a ‘wave of hate’ and ‘anti-Muslim prejudice,’ NewsBusters executive editor Tim Graham told Fox News Digital.

The Times’ published a story headlined, "After 9/11, Islamophobia Shaped a Generation of Muslim New Yorkers," that said the "attacks unleashed a wave of hate, but the years since have seen Muslim Americans’ political and cultural influence grow."

LIBERAL VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT: DON'T LINK 9/11 TERROR ATTACKS TO 'ISLAM OR MUSLIMS'

Times reporters Liam Stack and Maya King wrote about "once-friendly neighbors" allegedly keeping their distance from American Muslims on the heels of the terror attacks, suggesting that many "have faced a quarter-century of suspicion and hostility."

"In New York, a generation of Muslim New Yorkers responded to the Islamophobia by organizing their communities: Mosques hosted makeshift legal clinics. Small businesses became hubs in a citywide civil rights network. Muslims of different racial, ethnic and linguistic backgrounds formed alliances the city had not seen before," Stack and King wrote.

"Their political organizing helped, years later, to elect the city’s first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani," they continued. "But anti-Muslim prejudice still endures, echoing the Islamophobia that arose in the earliest days after Sept. 11."

The Times’ story, which was published hours before the somber anniversary of the attacks that killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon and aboard United Flight 93 near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, said the attacks also "left many Muslim American communities scarred by heavy-handed law enforcement tactics and the suspicion, if not outright hostility, of classmates, co-workers, elected officials and cable news commentators who blamed all Muslims for the terrorism they, too, had experienced that day."

MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'

The Times then spoke with Afaf Nasher, the executive director of the New York chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, who said that Muslim Americans were "pushed against the wall" and were faced with the decision to "run in fear" or push back.

"Political empowerment was certainly one way that we are pushing back," Nasher told the Gray Lady.

Stack and King noted that the ascendance of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani "has turned New York into perhaps the most prominent example of American Muslim success in the post-9/11 world" before suggesting Muslims in the United States continue to face many challenges.

"Those include a history of police surveillance, backlash faced by high-profile Muslims in politics or the arts, and attacks on Islamic religious expression, including the construction of mosques and the wearing of religious clothing like hijabs. Those biases have also affected followers of other faiths, in particular observant Sikh men, whose turbans are often mistaken for a form of Islamic dress," Stack and King wrote.

MAMDANI HEADS TO 9/11 MEMORIAL DESPITE 110,000-SIGNATURE PUSH FROM VICTIMS’ FAMILIES TO STAY AWAY

"After Sept. 11, many Muslims in New York found themselves under covert police surveillance," they continued.

The report evoked a Pew Research Center survey that found some American adults believe Muslims are less patriotic than other Americans, and they often cite the Sept. 11 attacks as the reason.

"By some measures, the survey showed that public attitudes toward Islam were more negative now than they were immediately after the attacks," Stack and King wrote.

Graham, who has put a spotlight on bias in the media for decades, said that "any surveillance of Muslims or mosques is treated as prejudice, despite the obvious point that some mosques and their leaders support Islamist terrorism."

CBC RELEASES POLICY CHANGE AFTER CONTROVERSY ABOUT REFUSING TO REFER TO 9/11 AS ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’

"’Islamophobia’ is always an oppressive problem that America needs to overcome, and increasing political and cultural influence of Muslim leftists like Zohran Mamdani was treated like signs of progress. For people who claim to oppose organized hate, they can't seem to find any in Muslim circles," Graham said.

Overall, you're only presented with pro-Muslim gush," Graham continued. "There is no opposing point of view, just a citation of hatred and prejudice from Trump and the Republicans."

Graham and other critics pointed out that the Times published a second story on Islamophobia on Friday, with the other one headlined, "Facing Islamophobia, Mamdani Keeps Focus on 9/11 Victims."

Conservative critics took to social media to blast the Times.

The Times stood by its reporting. 

"This misleading statement is nothing more than a disingenuous attempt to seek attention and stoke outrage by misrepresenting The New York Times's journalism covering the anniversary and commemoration of the Sept. 11 attacks. In the 25 years since that day, we have led the way on reporting on the event, its human toll, and resulting societal shifts. Audiences can see for themselves The Times's coverage now, which features a deep and diverse set of journalism reflecting on a globally significant event," a New York Times spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

item.title: Inside Trump’s intimate meeting with nation’s bravest soldiers during whirlwind Texas trip
item.description: Trump toured the new National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, then signed legislation for a new monument near the Lincoln Memorial.
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — During his whirlwind trip to Texas to rally Republican voters ahead of November’s elections, President Donald Trump on Thursday made a pit stop to honor America’s bravest warriors the day before the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

The intimate gathering was held at the National Medal of Honor Museum, where Trump also met privately with the Medal of Honor recipients who were present.

Trump also signed legislation clearing the way for a new monument honoring the award's recipients on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., before addressing roughly 100 guests, including 16 of the nation’s 65 living Medal of Honor recipients.

REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG

"It’s very special for all of us," Trump said. "It's special for me to be here, and it's an American treasure devoted to the best and bravest warriors of our country. And frankly, it's really the best they've ever produced."

The event was a stark contrast to the tens of thousands to whom Trump had addressed about 13 hours prior at the GOP midterm convention, a half hour away in Dallas.

DAVID MARCUS: IN DALLAS, GOP SEEKS UNITY ON 9/11, KIRK ANNIVERSARIES

Charlotte Jones, daughter of Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, is the chairman of the museum’s board of directors and served as the event’s emcee. Her father beamed with pride as he sat front-and-center, which Trump noted from the stage.

High-ranking Republican politicians, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, were among the high-profile guests who huddled in the room for the event.

Both Jones and Troy Bertram, the CEO of the new center, stressed that the National Medal of Honor Museum (NMOH) typical is not just a war museum.

"We are not a military history museum," Bertram told Fox News Digital. "We are storytelling around the humans, about their courage, their sacrifice. Who they were before what they became."

Trump’s speech struck a tone of admiration for the men honored by the museum.

MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH'

"They stormed into hellfire and crushed America's enemies," the president said. "They had bravery like few people could even think of having. They carried the wounded out of battle and on their own backs, and carried them back and forth … They stood in the way of bullets, purposely just standing just like this and taking bullets, and it's amazing."

One of those warriors in question was Army Lt. Col. William Swenson, a man of steely resolve who serves on the museum’s board.

DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

His heroic 2009 actions in Afghanistan, where he fought during Operation Enduring Freedom, earned him the highest military decoration awarded by the U.S. government in 2013, presented by then-President Barack Obama.

Pinned down by the enemy during a seven-hour battle in the Ganjgal Valley of the country’s Kunar Province, Swenson saved lives by making multiple trips into active combat zones, pulling wounded soldiers to safety and loading them onto helicopters for evacuation.

"The president and our commander-in-chief has been a strong supporter of this project," Swenson told Fox News Digital. "He continues to be a strong supporter of this project, and having him as involved as he is going to be a great contribution to get the monument done to standard, on time and to start signaling the messaging to the American people what’s important about service."

The 47th president is working with private donors to build the new monument in Washington, D.C., near the Lincoln Memorial, in honor of recipients of nation’s highest military award for heroism in battle. He previously signed the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act, officially clearing the path for its construction.

WWII VET GIVES DIRECT MESSAGE TO YOUNG PEOPLE TODAY: 'WE GAVE UP OUR YESTERDAYS FOR YOUR TOMORROWS'

"When he died, Woody was the last surviving recipient from World War II, [he] had one of the most dangerous jobs of war, and that’s operating a flamethrower," Trump said, speaking of the man for whom the bill was named.

"In the Battle of Iwo Jima, he carved a path to American victory — literally carved a path so soldiers could get in and win through a deadly gauntlet of enemy strongholds. And back and forth he went. He just kept going back and forth," Trump continued.

Williams was one of about 300 flamethrowers in Iwo Jima, a famed and defining battle in the war’s pacific theater. The late soldier’s family members were in the audience, and were fondly acknowledged by the president.

"America will never, ever forget what they did and what they risked and how much they risked, [and] what they meant to their families and what they've meant to our country, Trump concluded. "I want to thank you all once again."

Swenson described the importance of remembrance.

"What we do to ensure that we have common history, common beliefs, is we have monuments and we have museums, we have our mythology that tells us who we are as Americans and what we will continue to be in the future," he said. "Without this mythology, we don’t have that narrative.

The fact that the event was held the day before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 wasn’t lost on him, either.

He described the tragedy as a "seminal event" for him, which happened just as he was finishing college, that shaped his entire future. Swenson spent 22 years in the Army following the attack.

"The United States is forged in fire," he said. "We’ve had revolutions, we’ve had civil wars, we’ve had global conflicts, we’ve had civil strife. There will always be challenges to our freedom and to our country, and it’s up to us to move forward from those events and create that more perfect union."

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

"That said, we must always learn from these events to help better prevent them, and also to honor the sacrifice of the service members who fought in these conflicts, and also understand how we as citizens can create a better country that does not have these problems — that does not have these challenges. It’s our responsibility to future generations to prevent that."

item.title: OutKick's Craig Carton rips Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers: 'He's a lousy person'
item.description: Aaron Rodgers made shocking claims about ex-fiancée Shailene Woodley and Danica Patrick on the Cam Heyward podcast, drawing sharp criticism.
item.content:encoded:
Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers is a rather divisive, polarizing figure in sports.

Some people love his brash honesty and anti-establishment takes while others can't stand his hardened exterior and surly demeanor.

You can file OutKick's Craig Carton under the latter category, as he took Mr. Rodgers (whom he calls "The LeBron James of the NFL") to task over his latest controversial comments he made on a podcast appearance with Steelers teammate Cam Heyward.

AARON RODGERS ROASTS 'GUTLESS' ESPN'S INTEGRITY FOR ITS DIANNA RUSSINI-MIKE VRABEL COVERAGE 'HYPOCRISY'

Rodgers was quoted as saying that his ex-fiance, Hollywood actress Shailene Woodly, told him that she needed to "go f–k this guy" just days after she agreed to marry the star signal caller.

Carton took exception to this.

"Mr. Narcissist himself, Aaron Rodgers, went on the Cam Heyward Podcast, and decided that this was the right platform to embarrass himself," Carton retorted.

As Carton points out, Woodley hasn't spoken about Rodgers publicly for almost two years, yet the Super Bowl MVP feels the need to bring something up that may not have even happened in the first place.

CRAIG CARTON, MICHAEL RAPAPORT DISH ON THEIR SHARED DISLIKE FOR LEBRON JAMES: 'DEAD TO ME'

"Just because Aaron Rodgers said it, doesn’t mean it’s true," Carton explained.

"The more he protests all the accusations against him, and the criticism of him, the more I gathered the fact that he’s a weird guy, a high maintenance guy, an absolute narcissist, and a guy that women should stay thousands of yards away from."

But Rodgers didn't stop with Woodley, and turned his sights towards former NASCAR driver Danica Patrick and her lack of intimacy during their relationship, as it would appear no ex is safe from his wrath.

He also claimed that Patrick was depressed after retiring from auto racing, and refused to let her help pay for his house in Malibu, saying he didn't think the relationship was going in the right direction.

AARON RODGERS CLEARS AIR ON 'RACY' DREW ALLAR DM RUMORS ON CAM HEYWARD PODCAST: 'IT'S NOT TRUE'

While there doesn't seem to be any extrinsic motivation for Rodgers to make these comments, given neither of these women have spoken publicly about him in quite some time, Carton opines this all ties back to his narcissism.

"What joy do you get out of embarrassing Danica Patrick publicly? What joy do you get out of embarrassing Shailene Woodley publicly," he asked. "It’s always about you, isn't it, Aaron?"

Rodgers even threw some of his former teammates under the bus, and although he wouldn't refer to them by name, Carton was able to identify them as former Packers receiver Greg Jennings and tight end Jermichael Finley.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

He bad mouths his exes, he bad mouths his former teammates, and although he will be a no-doubter for the Pro Football Hall of Fame, he's certainly not a hall of fame human, if Carton has anything to say about it.

"As great as Aaron Rodgers was…he’s a lousy person," he explained. "And when it all comes down in the wash, would you rather be a great football player or a great person?"

item.title: Asked Siri to call your bank? A scam could cost thousands
item.description: Asking Siri to call American Express connected an 82-year-old woman to a bogus number that nearly drained $100,000 from her Bank of America account.
item.content:encoded:
Asking Siri to call your credit card company sounds about as routine as asking for the weather. You say the company name, Siri finds a number and the call begins. For Virginia, an 82-year-old woman from Concord, Massachusetts, that simple request nearly turned into a financial nightmare.

She says she asked Siri to call American Express. Instead, she reached a bogus number. From there, the conversation eventually moved to her Bank of America account and a supposed $1,000 credit that suddenly became $100,000. Virginia caught on before sending the money.

Her story shows how a Siri bank scam can exploit something many of us barely think about: where a phone number came from before we dialed it. The Better Business Bureau has previously warned that fake customer service numbers can surface through voice searches. It has documented cases involving Siri and other voice assistants where people believed they had reached a legitimate company.

Here's how the scam unfolded and what you can do before your next financial call to make sure you're reaching the real company.

FTC REVEALS WHERE SPAM CALLS HIT HARDEST

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money Replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

Virginia wrote to CyberGuy after the experience because she wanted other people to know how quickly a seemingly safe phone call can go wrong.

"Hi, I just wanted to pass on this scam. I needed to call American Express. Instead of using the phone number on my credit card, I asked Siri to call American Express instead. It was all downhill from that point on. The telephone number was bogus, and eventually I wound up on my BOA account with a so-called BOA Security Expert. Fortunately, when zeros started being added to the $1000.00 credit I was supposed to get, and the "gentleman" said he couldn't correct it, I needed to go to BOA and return the $100000.00. I realized what was going on and immediately hung up and froze my BOA account. I never expected that a number that Siri provided would lead to trouble. I try to inform people now that calling a number can also put your finances in jeopardy. I am 82 years old and could have lost my entire retirement in one fell swoop. Thank you," Virginia, Concord, Massachusetts.

That last part stopped me. Virginia had no reason to think asking Siri to place a call could potentially put her retirement savings in danger. After all, she initiated the call herself. That gave the person who answered an immediate advantage.

Based on Virginia's account, this looks like two scam techniques chained together. First came the fake customer service number. Then came a refund or overpayment scheme designed to persuade her to send real money back.

Virginia says she asked Siri to call American Express rather than using the phone number printed on her card. Apple says business information can appear across Apple services, including Maps and Siri. Place cards can include phone numbers and other business details.

We reached out to Apple for comment but did not hear back before our deadline. However, Virginia's experience alone cannot tell us how this specific bogus number became associated with her request. We simply do not know how the bad number got there.

This was a powerful setup because Virginia believed she had contacted American Express herself. She had not answered a random phone call. She had asked her iPhone to make the call. That can lower your guard before the person on the other end even says hello.

The Better Business Bureau has warned about this problem. Scammers can promote fake support numbers that make their way into online search results. Voice assistants may then use information pulled from those results or related business listings.

We have seen a similar trap with traditional web searches. In our report, The No. 1 Google search scam everyone falls for, a victim searching for customer support landed on a fake number and eventually lost control of his phone. Voice assistants can add another layer of trust because you may never see the number before the call starts.

According to Virginia, she eventually found herself dealing with someone claiming to be a Bank of America security expert. At that point, the story had shifted from customer service to her bank account. That shift should immediately raise your guard. Bank of America warns about criminals who pose as bank representatives and invent urgent problems involving your account. Scammers may ask for verification codes, remote access or money transfers. Then Virginia encountered the clue that saved her.

Virginia says she expected a $1,000 credit. Then zeros started appearing. Suddenly, she was dealing with $100,000. The supposed bank expert told her the mistake could not be corrected. According to Virginia, she was then told she needed to go to Bank of America and return the excess money. That follows a familiar overpayment or refund scam pattern.

Scammers claim they accidentally sent too much money. Then they pressure you to return the difference before you have time to verify what happened. Fortunately, the sudden jump to $100,000 made Virginia question the entire story. She hung up and froze her Bank of America account.

We cannot determine that from Virginia's description. Scammers sometimes use remote-access software to manipulate what a person sees on a computer. They can also move a victim's own money between accounts, so it appears that a new deposit arrived. Another possibility involves a fake banking page designed to display whatever balance the criminal wants the victim to see.

CyberGuy has covered how fake support representatives use remote access and other tactics to take control of devices. You can see the warning signs in our guide, Protect yourself from tech support scams. Virginia did not provide enough information to identify the exact technique used here.

What we do know is that the criminal wanted her to believe $100,000 had appeared and that she needed to return it. If she had followed those instructions, the money she sent would have been very real.

NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

A scammer may know your name, your bank or details that make the call sound convincing. These steps can help you stay in control.

For banks and credit card companies, the safest starting point is usually the number printed on the back of your physical card. You can also open the institution's official app and find its contact information there. Avoid relying on a phone number supplied by a search result, sponsored ad or voice assistant when your finances are involved.

A call to your credit card company should not suddenly require you to move money through an unrelated bank account. If the story starts getting complicated, hang up. Then contact the company again using a verified number.

A scammer may claim your money needs to be transferred into another account to keep it safe. Do not do it. Bank of America warns that it will never ask customers to transfer money because fraud was detected on an account. The same caution applies if someone tells you to withdraw cash, buy gift cards or purchase cryptocurrency to resolve a banking problem.

If someone says $1,000 accidentally became $100,000, stop. Do not transfer the supposed difference back. Contact your bank independently and ask it to verify your actual balance and transaction history.

Banks use one-time codes to confirm your identity or approve certain actions. A scammer may ask you to read one aloud while claiming it is needed to cancel fraud. Never give a verification code to someone who called you or someone you reached through an unverified number.

If someone claiming to represent a bank or credit card company tells you to install software that lets them see or control your screen, end the call. Remote-access programs can give criminals enormous control over your computer. They may watch you log into your bank, move money between accounts or manipulate what appears on the screen.

Strong antivirus software can help protect you if a fake support representative sends you to a malicious website or convinces you to download a dangerous file. It can also warn you about phishing pages and other threats designed to steal passwords or financial information. The best way to safeguard yourself from malicious links that install malware, potentially accessing your private information, is to have antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, keeping your personal information and digital assets safe. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Set alerts for purchases, withdrawals and transfers so you know quickly when money moves. You should also enable notifications for suspicious logins and changes to your account information when your financial institution offers them. These alerts give you another chance to catch activity you did not authorize.

Your banking password should never be reused on another account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so you do not have to remember them all. Also enable two-factor authentication whenever your bank supports it. An authenticator app or security key can provide stronger protection when available.

If someone tells you money suddenly appeared in your account, do not rely on what they show you. Close the session. Open your bank's official app yourself or type the bank's website address directly into your browser. Then check your transactions independently.

If Siri or Apple Maps provides incorrect business information, you can report the listing to Apple. On an iPhone, open Maps > tap your picture or initials next to the search field > tap Reports > tap Report a New Issue > choose the appropriate option and follow the on-screen instructions. Fixing a bad listing may help prevent someone else from reaching the same number.

APPLE’S $250M SIRI SETTLEMENT: ARE YOU OWED CASH?

If you think a scammer got access to your financial information, act quickly.

Hang up and stop responding to texts, emails or calls from the person. Do not use a callback number they provided.

Use the number on your card or inside the official app. Tell the fraud department exactly what happened. Ask whether any transfers, new payees or other account changes need to be stopped.

Virginia froze her Bank of America account as soon as she realized something was wrong. Your bank may also allow you to lock a debit or credit card instantly through its app.

If you entered a password while the scammer could see your screen, or you gave one away, change it from a trusted device. Change any other account that used the same or a similar password.

If you installed a remote-control program at the scammer's direction, disconnect that computer from the internet. Remove the software and run a full antivirus scan before signing back into sensitive accounts. If you are unsure whether the device is clean, get help from a trusted computer professional before using it for banking again.

Look for unfamiliar transactions, new payees and changes to your phone number or email address. Also check whether the scammer altered security settings or added a new device to the account.

If the scammer obtained your Social Security number or enough personal information to open accounts in your name, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open new credit in your name.

Report financial fraud to your bank immediately. You can also file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If money was transferred, contact the financial institution involved as soon as possible. Some transactions become much harder to recover once they are completed.

Criminals may contact victims again after the first attempt. Sometimes they pretend to be investigators, bank employees or recovery specialists who claim they can get your money back. Treat any unexpected follow-up contact with suspicion.

What sticks with me about Virginia's story is how ordinary the first move felt. She was trying to reach a company she already trusted and used Siri to save herself a little time. That tiny convenience nearly opened the door to a six-figure loss. Virginia also deserves credit for catching the moment when the story stopped making sense. A $1,000 credit becoming $100,000 was enough to make her question the person guiding her. 

That instinct protected her retirement. I also would not frame this as an age issue. Criminals succeed because they exploit trust in familiar technology and recognizable financial brands. Anyone can get caught when a call begins through a device they use every day. From now on, I would treat financial phone numbers almost like passwords. Verify them before you use them. The number on your physical card or inside the official banking app gives you a much stronger starting point than a search result or voice request.

After hearing what happened to Virginia, would you still let Siri dial your bank without checking the number first? Have you ever reached the wrong company through a voice assistant or online search? item.title: 'Very hot' coffee and tea linked to higher cancer risk in nearly 1 million adults
item.description: A University of Oxford study of nearly 1 million adults links very hot tea and coffee to a threefold higher risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
item.content:encoded:
Regularly drinking very hot tea or coffee may raise the risk of a type of esophageal cancer, according to a large study at the University of Oxford.

People who reported drinking beverages "very hot" had about three times the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), a type of cancer that begins in the cells lining the esophagus, compared to those who drank warm beverages.

Drinking six or more hot drinks per day was associated with a 71% higher risk of the disease. The same link was not seen for esophageal adenocarcinoma (AC), a type of cancer that develops in the lower part of the esophagus.

ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

The study included nearly 1 million U.K. adults, making it the largest investigation of its kind to date, according to lead study author Keren Papier, a nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford.

Roughly half of the participants were from the Million Women Study (MWS), who were followed for an average of 14 years, and the other half were from the UK Biobank (UKB), who were followed for 11 years.

"Compared with people who reported drinking their beverages ‘warm,’ those who drank them ‘hot’ had around a 1.7 times higher risk of SCC, while those who drank them ‘very hot’ had around a three times higher risk," Papier told Fox News Digital.

The study was published in the International Journal of Cancer.

FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

The researchers estimated that, if the observed association reflects a true cause-and-effect relationship, about 14% of SCC cases could potentially be prevented if people drank beverages "hot" rather than "very hot."

The biggest limitation, according to the researchers, is that beverage temperatures were self-reported rather than directly measured. Because people's tolerance for heat differs, participants may have classified similar temperatures differently.

"A limitation of our study was that, although we examined associations by self-reported preferred drink temperature, we did not have data on directly measured drink temperatures, and, therefore, cannot determine how self-reported drink temperature is likely to relate to absolute drink temperature," Papier noted.

"These findings don't mean people need to stop drinking tea or coffee. Just let your drinks cool down a little before drinking them."

An outside cancer specialist agreed the findings are biologically plausible but said they should be interpreted in context.

Dr. Aaron Sasson, chief of surgical oncology and co-director of the gastrointestinal oncology team at Stony Brook Cancer Center in New York, said it’s been known that drinking hot beverages or liquids can be irritating to the esophagus and that it could contribute to the development of esophageal cancer.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The hotter the liquid, the higher the risk of a "thermal injury," the doctor told Fox News Digital.

"Similar to burning your hand, if you were to get a burn on your hand, you have an increased risk of getting squamous cell carcinoma of the hand, of the skin developing in the burned area," Sasson said. "So, think of that as constantly repeating a burn to the esophagus."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The doctor reiterated that this study specifically looked at the risk of squamous carcinomas, not adenocarcinomas.

"In the United States, about 85% of all of our cancers are adenocarcinomas. So, the incidence of squamous carcinomas in the esophagus is quite low, just to put it into perspective," he noted.

The lifetime risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus in the U.S. is less than 1%, the doctor said.

Sasson agreed that there was no "objective measurement" of the drinks’ temperature, which poses an unknown variable.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If you are a heavy consumer of hot tea or coffee, maybe you'd want to cool it down a little bit," he advised. "But I think, for practical purposes, for most people, [it’s] not the predominant risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus."

Smoking, heavy alcohol use, acid reflux and obesity are among the better-established risk factors for esophageal cancer, Sasson said.

"If you were to limit alcohol consumption and eliminate cigarette smoking, you will have done wonders for your esophagus."

item.title: USS Cole commander recalls chilling 9/11 warning at CIA just 20 minutes before first plane hit
item.description: Kirk Lippold warned CIA officials that a catastrophic attack was coming just 20 minutes before the first plane struck the World Trade Center.
item.content:encoded:
Just 20 minutes before the first hijacked plane struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, the USS Cole's former commander made a chilling prediction inside CIA headquarters.

Speaking on the "Fox News Rundown" podcast commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11, retired Navy Commander Kirk Lippold said the moment at Langley underscores a lesson he believes the nation cannot afford to forget.

Lippold said he had just finished a briefing with a senior CIA official about intelligence related to the USS Cole attack. When asked for his assessment, Lippold warned that it would likely take a catastrophic event on U.S. soil for the American people to recognize the threat.

FOR 'HORRIBLE MOMENT,' BUSH WHITE HOUSE THOUGHT US MILITARY SHOT DOWN FLIGHT 93

"I said, 'I'm [going to] be honest with you, sir. America doesn't understand. I believe it is going to take a seminal event probably in this country where hundreds, if not thousands, died before Americans realized that we are at war with this guy,' meaning [Osama] bin Laden," Lippold told Fox News' Lucas Tomlinson.

"Twenty minutes after I said that, the first plane hit the North Tower, and I was literally leaving the headquarters when the plane hit the South Tower."

25 YEARS LATER, 9/11 MEMORIES ENDURE AS NATION GATHERS TO HONOR NEARLY 3,000 LIVES LOST

The 9/11 terror attacks killed nearly 3,000 people, and thousands more have died from related illnesses. Less than a year before that day, Lippold was the commanding officer of the USS Cole when al Qaeda terrorists attacked the guided-missile destroyer.

On Oct. 12, 2000, two suicide bombers in a small boat pulled alongside the ship in Aden, Yemen, offering friendly gestures before detonating explosives in their boat alongside the Cole. Seventeen U.S. sailors were killed, and 37 others were injured in the blast, which ripped a hole near the ship's waterline.

AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11; THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

That incident was one of several al Qaeda attacks in the years leading up to 9/11, including the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings in East Africa, when Lippold argues went largely unanswered by U.S. leadership. For Lippold, watching the Pentagon burn on 9/11 reinforced his belief that the United States must aggressively confront terrorist groups around the globe.

"It really solidified to me the costs that if the United States does not react to the threat of terrorism and countries who support it, we will continue to pay a price in the future," Lippold said.

9/11 WIDOW TERRY STRADA ACCUSES US OF PROTECTING SAUDI ARABIA 25 YEARS AFTER TERROR ATTACKS, ADDRESSES VANCE

"And it really doesn't matter whether it is through the drugs, whether it's through actually [an] attack, through waterborne or vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices, terrorism has to be ruthlessly stopped anywhere around the world," he added.

item.title: Fans fume at NFL for being 'un-American,' Sophie the sex symbol & the greatest post-9/11 national anthem ever
item.description: Football Friday kicks off with NFL fans furious over the Rams-49ers Netflix game in Australia and Jim Cornelison's powerful 9/11 anthem moment.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Our first 'Football Friday' of the year with all participants. We've made it! Friday night lights tonight. A full slate of college football tomorrow.

And, of course, the NFL returns on Sunday. RedZone. The "Witching Hour." The Fox and CBS theme songs. Carrie Underwood back in our living rooms Sunday night as we all attempt to win back our money after a day of horrible gambling beats.

Who has it better than us? What a country. What a big, beautiful, perfect country.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS

And that's important to remember today. It's the 25th anniversary of 9/11. A quarter-century has passed since the world changed forever, and we're still trying to find our way back.

We'll get into it today — just a bit — before returning to our regularly-scheduled programming.

Let's roll.

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where NFL fans spent the evening trying to figure out how to find the Rams-49ers game on Netflix. They're not happy today.

NFL ANNOUNCES INAUGURAL THANKSGIVING EVE GAME BETWEEN PACKERS AND RAMS WILL BE STREAMED ON NETFLIX

I don't blame them.

What else? I've got some 9/11 thoughts, including the best national anthem you've ever heard, and did anyone catch the Miami-FAMU game last night?

Buddy, you haven't LIVED until you bet on a football team to score OVER 0.5 points in a game where they are so clearly overmatched, you start to feel bad for them about five minutes into it.

What a rush!

Grab you whatever you need to get you though the final day of the work week — dealer's choice today! — and settle in for a Friday 'Cap.

Before we get into the serious stuff, I'd like to go ahead and start with last night's blowout in Australia. The Rams looked lifeless. The Niners looked like a Super Bowl juggernaut (even though they refused to give Christian McCaffrey the ball).

The game, of course, was on Netflix, which means half the country couldn't find it. The setting itself was cool, but it felt ... weird.

Right?

Anyone else get that feeling?

The seats inside this giant stadium were miles away from the actual field. Could you imagine buying a ticket, and THIS is your view?

Yikes. You could hear the difference back here in the states, too. There was NO crowd pop. At all. Go back and listen to the Pats-Seahawks game from Wednesday, and then compare it to last night's crowd.

It sounds like a different sport.

Look, I know what the NFL and Roger Goodell is trying to do with these international games. I get it. Expand, expand, expand! These owners and commissioners, in every league, are just obsessed with expanding their reach.

SOLD OUT MELBOURNE CROWD STANDS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY COMMEMORATION OF 9/11 AT NFL'S FIRST AUSTRALIA GAME

But good Lord, can't we just keep the NFL in the US of A? Football doesn't need expansion. It's the most popular sport in America, by a wide margin. Why do we need to grow the game outside the country?

That side of the world doesn't need football. They have futbol. And they are FINE with it. We should be, too.

Keep the NFL in America. Enough of these international games. It's nonsense.

"Absolute crazy work for the NFL to put this game in Australia and behind a Netflix paywall. Completely out of reach and un-American."

That's my biggest takeaway from last night's game. That was, clearly, the biggest takeaway from NFL fans back here in the states. Folks were DONE with it by halftime, and I don't blame them.

It's the same argument I have when these college teams go to a neutral site for a game. STOP it. You wanna know what makes college football great? The campus atmosphere. Quit going to these giant neutral site stadiums for big games.

And stop going overseas to play an NFL game. We appreciate it way more back home. Trust me.

Now, while the country was unified against the NFL's decision last night, we were unified in a much different way 15 years ago.

If you watch ONE sports-related thing about 9/11 today, watch this clip of Jim Cornelison singing the national anthem on the 10th anniversary of the attacks.

It's perfect:

Goodness gracious. The best national anthem performance ... ever? Just listen to that crowd. Usually, we're all reserved and quiet for the anthem, out of respect.

There are occasions, though, where our emotions take over. This day, every year, is one of those occasions.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I was in third grade when the towers were struck. I don't remember really anything from when I was 8. Bits and pieces, but not much.

I remember that day. Always have.

I remember our teacher putting the news on in our classroom. I remember school getting out early, because America was under attack and we had no idea who was next.

I remember coming home and walking into our living room, and my mom was watching NBC, on those GIANT, flimsy flat-screens from the late-90s, and just sobbing.

I remember having no idea what was happening. But also, at the same time, knowing something was very wrong.

Folks who were born pre and post-9/11 live two very different lives. I assume it's the same with the Kennedy assassination.

It's easy to forget who we were that day. How we responded. We've lost so much of that in 2026. Everyone is so angry, and so tense, and so combative.

I choose to remember how unified this country was in the days, weeks, months and years after those attacks.

Goodness, I hope we can get back to that one day. Sooner rather than later, preferably.

OK, let's get the morale back on track and rapid-fire this Friday class into a big football weekend. First up? Anyone see the 'Canes game last night?

Lordy. 77-7. Could've been 177-7, if Miami wanted it. Seriously. The Hurricanes were favored by 50, and somehow covered with ease. FAMU's team total was set at 0.5.

Yes. You read that right. Zero. Point. Five.

Because I'm a lunatic, I took that bet. And buddy, it was an ELECTRIC cash:

CHA-CHING! I've never been so locked in on a FAMU score in my life. I doubt I ever will be again.

Hat's off to the Rattlers for playing all four quarters.

As for Miami ... good job? I guess? I personally don't think those two teams have any business being on the same field together ever again, especially during the NIL era.

We have to have some standards, right? Goodness.

OK, that's it for today — and this week!

On the way out, here's Sophie Cunningham breaking her silence with Colin Cowherd and admitting she's perfectly fine being a sex symbol, as Colin put it.

Don't listen to the haters and the losers, Sophie! Do you.

See y'all Monday.

item.title: Kamala Harris claims GOP 'cheating' ahead of midterms, says she's focused on stopping the 'madness'
item.description: Former Vice President Kamala Harris accused Republicans of "cheating" by redrawing lines and suppressing votes, telling Megan Rapinoe she's focused on winning midterms.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris accused Republicans of "cheating" during an interview Thursday and said she was working to "stop the madness" by helping Democrats win the midterm elections.

"Midterms, midterms, midterms, full-time occupying my thoughts, my mind and my work," Harris said. 

"We have to win these midterms. These — these folks are cheating. They're redrawing lines. They're trying to make it more difficult for people to vote so they won't vote because they are afraid of the power of the people.

"And, so, I'm spending full-time working on doing everything I can to help people restore some balance in our government, which is, through the midterms, winning back Congress, the House and the Senate so that we can stop the madness," Harris told former women's soccer star Megan Rapinoe on her podcast, "What Are You Like?"

KAMALA HARRIS DIVES INTO MIDTERM FIGHT ONLY TO GET ROASTED FOR NEVER HAVING 'AN ORIGINAL THOUGHT IN HER LIFE’

Rapinoe asked Harris about what brought her back into political and public life.

"I don't know how to live and not serve. I honestly don't. I just don't. It's something I've come to terms with. I don't know how to, I just don't know a life without figuring out how I can help move the needle," she said.

Harris said she wanted to restore "some sense of sanity" and a functioning government.

"If Kamala Harris is upset Republicans are going after the illegals and fraudsters trying to vote, it makes you wonder if she's taking crazy pills again. Voter ID and proof of citizenship are common sense, but Democrats can’t win elections without cheating the system," RNC election integrity Communications Director Ally Triolo told Fox News Digital in a statement.

FOX NEWS POLL: SIGNIFICANT SUPPORT FOR BOTH VOTER ID LAWS AND MAIL-IN BALLOTS

Rapinoe also asked the former vice president if she had made a decision about running in 2028.

"I haven't decided," Harris said. "From my perspective, '28 doesn't matter if we don't win '26."

Harris said during an interview last week with MS NOW's Peter Alexander that she even supported Democrats who don't want her on the campaign trail with them, because, she said, they need to do whatever it takes to win.

"Listen, Peter, we need to win, OK? Bottom line, we need to win," Harris said. "I have run locally, I’ve run for statewide office and, obviously, nationally. And these candidates know what they need to do to win, and I would expect nothing less.

"I look forward to being on the trail and helping folks where I can be helpful, but we have got to put a check on this lawless administration and deliver what Americans need and deserve. Lower costs, affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, you name it. So, I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win."

KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN

Rapinoe also discussed her experience as a female athlete.

"I’m thinking about my own experience being a female athlete, and I went through, in the prime of my career, just the most historic time in women’s sports," she said. "I mean, it was crazy in the best ways. We saw a huge amount of progress, which has led into a pretty significant regression in terms of just equal rights and people’s rights in general. I definitely think those two are tied.

"It was for the longest time, you know, don't talk about women's issues," she added. "Same kind of thing. It was like, 'Well, you're not that good,' or 'You're not that entertaining' or, 'Don't do it like this or whatever.'

"And then we did it, and all women's sports sort of did it. And then it was like, 'OK, we're just going to do something else.' And I always just felt like they're like they're not going to let us just win."

item.title: California woman chased, fatally shot by illegal immigrant DoorDash driver who stalked her for months: DHS
item.description: DHS says Shalini Thakur's fatal Sacramento shooting was preventable if Biden administration immigration policies hadn't released her alleged killer.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said a California woman was fatally shot outside a Sacramento County Panera Bread Tuesday by an illegal immigrant who had stalked her for months and was subject to a restraining order.

Shalini Thakur, 38, was standing near her car when Rohit Rohit, an illegal immigrant from India, approached her, chased her when she tried to flee and shot her in the head before getting in a car and driving away, DHS said.

Responding police officers caught up to him, but Rohit took his own life with a gun, according to authorities.

BIDEN ADMIN RELEASED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF FATALLY STABBING FAIRFAX COUNTY MOTHER

Rohit spent months stalking Thakur, who was eventually granted a restraining order. Thakur said she knew Rohit as a DoorDash delivery driver who would park outside her home for hours and talk to her on a daily basis, ABC 10 reported.

DEADLY HOSPITAL STABBING PUTS NEWSOM UNDER PRESSURE OVER ICE DETAINER FIGHT

Rohit had stalked Thakur since at least January, when she found an Apple AirTag under the hood of her car.

At one point, he tried to coerce her into marriage and prevented her from socializing with others, the news report said. He also allegedly threatened to shoot himself or anyone she met.

Rohit later deflated her car tires and followed her to work so he could pretend to offer her help, authorities said. At one point, Rohit allegedly obtained a copy of Thakur's apartment key so he could enter her home while she slept.

Even after she got a restraining order against Rohit in May, he continued to stalk her as recently as July.

"She could have been saved. She told police so many times," Thakur’s mother, Sudesh Kumari, told the news outlet. "She called them, but nobody did anything."

Rohit illegally entered the United States through Arizona in August 2023 and was arrested by U.S. Border Patrol. He was released as part of the Biden administration's policy to let migrants into the U.S. after they were given a court date to appear before a judge.

item.title: Dolly Parton could soon have major airport named in her honor after unanimous vote
item.description: Nashville's airport authority voted unanimously to begin renaming the airport after American icon Dolly Parton, though a final name has not yet been decided.
item.content:encoded:
Nashville International Airport is one step closer to undergoing a name change honoring late country music icon Dolly Parton.

The Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority voted unanimously, 6-0, Friday to begin the process of modifying the airport's name in Parton's honor, according to a statement from the authority.

The decision on the final name is still to come. 

DOLLY PARTON FANS CAN NOW BOOK STAYS AT HER UPCOMING HOTEL IN NASHVILLE

"While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton's name and legacy will be incorporated," the airport authority said.

Officials stressed that the vote marks only the beginning of the process  with more details expected in the coming months.

"This vote represents the first step in a multifaceted process," the airport authority said. "In the coming months, we anticipate having more definitive plans to share regarding the next steps and implementation."

The vote follows an earlier push to honor Parton at the airport after the Tennessee native died at age 80 last month.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Fox News Digital previously reported that Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Nashville International Airport announced plans in August to pursue naming the airport in Parton's honor.

Lee said at the time that he had spoken with Parton's team about the proposal and that her representatives were appreciative of the support and open to further discussions.

The effort also gained significant public support, with a petition calling for the airport to be renamed "Dolly Parton International Airport" drawing more than 155,000 verified signatures at the time of Fox News Digital's previous report.

Parton had deep ties to Tennessee throughout her life. She became one of the state's most recognizable figures through her music, philanthropy and Imagination Library literacy program.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The singer had previously resisted another effort to formally honor her in her home state.

In 2021, Parton asked Tennessee lawmakers to withdraw legislation that would have allowed a statue of her to be erected on the grounds of the state Capitol.

"I am honored and humbled by their intention, but I have asked the leaders of the state legislature to remove the bill from any and all consideration," Parton said at the time.

She did, however, leave open the possibility of such an honor in the future.

"I hope, though, that somewhere down the road, several years from now or perhaps after I'm gone, if you still feel I deserve it, then I'm certain I will stand proud in our great state Capitol as a grateful Tennessean."

Jasmine Baeher of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: AOC, Mamdani interaction caught on cam at 9/11 memorial sparks online fury
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were seen grinning at the 9/11 Memorial as a mourner sobbed nearby on camera.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., were lambasted Friday for appearing to share a moment of levity at the 9/11 Memorial in lower Manhattan during the solemn reading-of-the-names of victims.

Mamdani was already facing criticism from some 9/11 victims’ families over his attendance when a television feed showing the reading of victims’ names cut from a young man sobbing at the memorial to the mayor and congresswoman appearing to grin and laugh as they spoke, though their conversation was inaudible.

"Disgraceful," said Steve Guest, a former top staffer for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas. "AOC and Mamdani look happy."

ZOHRAN MAMDANI URGED TO SKIP NEW YORK CITY'S 9/11 MEMORIAL: 'VILE ANTISEMITE'

"While normal Americans cry, commie Mamdani and AOC laugh it up at the 9/11 memorial in New York," Pratt said.

RETIRED PORT AUTHORITY OFFICERS TELL MAMDANI, HOCHUL TO STAY AWAY FROM GROUND ZERO ON 9/11

Richard Sementa, better known as "Mr. Producer" for Mark Levin’s national radio show, tweeted, "Un-freaking believable."

Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., who continues to criticize democratic socialists and opponents of Israel, called the mayor "Jihad Mamdani" and said he and the congresswoman should not be anywhere near Ground Zero.

Separately, Mamdani was seen at other points standing somberly between New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and New York first gentleman William Hochul Jr.

But critics continued pointing out what one called the "jarring split-screen" of the mayor joking around with Ocasio-Cortez a split-second after the mourner was seen sobbing over the shadow "fountain" at the footprint of the Twin Towers.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: As Democrats protest in Dallas, conservatives are quiet and cautious
item.description: About 300 Democrats rallied at Dallas City Hall against Trump and the GOP, but quiet conservatives nearby tell a very different political story.
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday afternoon, former Democratic Party superstar Beto O’Rourke headlined a protest at Dallas City Hall that drew about 300 angry, loud Democrats and socialists convinced that in fighting against President Donald Trump and the GOP, they are saving America from fascism.

At the entrance to the event was a man holding a sign that read "MAGA = Fascist," complete with a swastika on it. And that was one of the nicer sentiments expressed in the homage signage seen around the event.

"I can’t stand the man. You cannot be a Christian while following that man," said Bonnie, an activist in her 60s, when asked why Trump provoked so much outright hatred.

DAVID MARCUS: AHEAD OF GOP CONVENTION, DALLAS DEMS SHARE WORRIED OPTIMISM

And it wasn’t just Trump. When asked about more generic Republicans like Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, or Sen. John Thune, R-N.D., Bonnie said, "If they allow him to do what he’s doing, they’re all in the same boat."

Rick, also post-retirement age, held a sign that read, "Conservatives Against Trump," and described his values as "small, limited government, a strong national defense and fiscal responsibility."

JOHN FETTERMAN DEFENDS TRUMP SUPPORTERS, CONDEMNS FELLOW DEMOCRATS' 'F--- TRUMP' STRATEGY

Asked whether he was concerned that the leftward lurch of the Democrats also threatened those centrist principles, Rick replied, "Clearly, both parties, both major parties, have become polarized."

From the stage came vitriol about everything from Jeffrey Epstein to data centers in the form of both speeches and song, while a small counterprotest was held at bay by Dallas police.

The theme of fascism was present on so many of the signs that I eventually asked one protester what they meant by the term, to which he simply replied, "If you don’t know then I can’t help you," which was not particularly clarifying.

The vocal zeal with which these protesters and other Democrats I met in Dallas denounce all things Republican stands in stark contrast with many of the conservatives I spoke to in the city, who, notwithstanding living in red Texas, tend to be a bit shy about their beliefs.

"At my son’s school, and around some friends, I just don’t bring up that I support Trump. It's just not worth it," said one woman, who asked to remain anonymous.

She also told me of friends she has who send out two sets of Christmas cards each year, one MAGA themed and one not. She now receives the former each holiday season.

Another man, who works in the service industry, said, "I can’t tell anyone at work that I like Trump. So, when it comes up, I just say that I’m a Bill Maher-style centrist." At least in his mind, that is as far to the right as he can publicly be without it causing problems.

It all reminded me of a young woman who I met last year who told me after we chatted that she didn’t know any conservatives and was surprised I was so nice. I asked her, "Do you have any guy friends who never ever talk about politics?" 

She said, "Yes," to which I replied, "Yeah, they’re conservative."

BILL MAHER'S DIRE MIDTERM ELECTION WARNING TO DEMS AFTER 'REALLY CRAZY' SOCIALISTS WIN PRIMARIES

I immediately felt a twinge of regret for outing them.

When Ronald Reagan was winning elections, pundits described his supporters as a silent majority; today, what we have may be something closer to a silenced majority, as conservatives hide their identities to avoid conflict.

This is a trend that I have discovered all across the country over the past few years: Praise of Trump seems always to come in a quiet whisper, criticism often loud enough for an entire room to hear.

One has to wonder, at a time when polling consistently overestimates support for Democrats, if this shy Trump voter phenomenon might be in play. After all, people trained to keep quiet about their politics may not be eager to respond to polls.

Many local Republican voters I spoke with are very nervous that this could be the year that Democrats finally flip Texas. But, in fairness, while they see myriad outward displays of affection for Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico, they may have no idea that their friend supports GOP candidate Ken Paxton.

The challenge for the Republican Party in this midterm cycle is to make sure that the Trump supporters who don’t want to admit it out loud will still show up to vote, making a difference despite their silence.

It is the quiet voters who are very likely to determine control of Congress, and whether the final two years of Trump’s presidency will be the solidification of his legacy or 24 long months of endless impeachment.

item.title: At Ground Zero, 9/11 families turn to Trump as Obama’s old decision resurfaces
item.description: Terry Strada accused successive administrations of protecting Saudi Arabia and urged Trump to release unredacted 9/11 files on the 25th anniversary.
item.content:encoded:
On a cloudy morning at the site where two sprawling towers once stood, the loved ones of New Yorkers killed on 9/11 gathered with a message for President Donald Trump: Release the unredacted files they believe could implicate Saudi Arabia.

Vice President JD Vance attended the ceremony alongside former presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, as well as former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Gov. Andrew Cuomo were also among those in attendance.

The message was delivered on the main stage by Terry Strada, whose husband, Tom, was killed in the attacks. Speaking from the memorial stage, Strada accused successive administrations of protecting Saudi Arabia instead of supporting the 9/11 families.

Strada called out President Barack Obama, who was at the memorial, for vetoing the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, or JASTA, in 2016. Congress later overrode the veto, allowing 9/11 families to sue Saudi Arabia over its alleged role in the attacks.

TRUMP SET TO HONOR 9/11 VICTIMS, FIRST RESPONDERS AT PENTAGON ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY

"Administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," Strada said. "They withheld evidence. They vetoed JASTA. They broke promises, both public and private. It has been one betrayal after another.

"President Trump can still change that"

She urged the president to tell Saudi leaders "that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through."

"Please carry that message back," another speaker said, addressing Vance. "Stand with the families. Stand with the survivors."

The remarks drew applause from the crowd.

"Administration after administration has not done anything for us. In fact, they've blocked, blocked us every step of the way of getting justice," Dennis McGinley, whose older brother Danny worked on the 89th floor of the South Tower, told Fox News Digital.

"President Trump has a unique, historic opportunity here to be a hero, be our champion, finally close the books on this American nightmare, which is now becoming an American embarrassment. It's got to start."

The appeal came as families marked the 25th anniversary of the attacks with a renewed push for accountability from Saudi Arabia, which they accuse of helping two of the hijackers establish themselves in the United States. The kingdom has repeatedly denied involvement.

The families’ claims center on Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national who helped hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar obtain an apartment in San Diego, and Fahad al-Thumairy, an accredited Saudi diplomat and imam at the King Fahd Mosque in California who had numerous contacts with al-Bayoumi.

The 9/11 Commission documented the men’s connections but did not conclude that the Saudi government or senior Saudi officials supported the plot. Its report also said investigators found no evidence that another Saudi national, Osama Bassnan, gave money to the hijackers.

Newly released investigative material and evidence presented in a long-running civil case have intensified scrutiny of those connections. In August 2025, U.S. District Judge George Daniels allowed claims against Saudi Arabia to proceed, finding that the families had presented enough evidence to move toward trial. The ruling did not determine that Saudi Arabia was responsible for the attacks.

The families say that legal ruling, along with additional FBI and British intelligence material, gives Trump an opportunity to release more records and help resolve what they view as a 25-year-old betrayal.

SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’

For Passananti, the demand was inseparable from his own loss. His father, Horace Robert Passananti, was working on the 100th floor of the North Tower. Passananti was 32 when he called his father after hearing that a plane had struck the building.

He never heard from him again.

Passananti said he has attended the ceremony every year but one since the attacks.

"I wish I wasn’t here, obviously, but I feel like I have to be here every year," he told Fox News Digital.

Passananti, who is affiliated with the group 9/11 Justice, said families want those responsible for the attacks held accountable.

"We’ve really been on our own — the families — trying to obtain evidence," Passananti said. "We’ve gotten really no help from our government. We feel like they’ve put Saudi Arabia ahead of the 9/11 families, and we’re hoping that will change."

TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

He described the delays in the case as "a twilight zone."

"It feels really like a twilight zone and unbelievable that we have to fight for justice for the worst terrorist attack that ever happened on our soil," Passananti said. "It doesn’t feel real. It’s unexplainable."

Trump has previously acknowledged that questions remain unanswered about the attacks. In 2022, while defending his decision to host a Saudi-backed LIV Golf tournament at his New Jersey club amid protests from 9/11 families, Trump said, "Nobody has gotten to the bottom of 9/11."

But Trump has not publicly said whether he supports releasing additional files concerning Saudi Arabia’s alleged ties to the hijackers.

McGinley worked across the Hudson River and called his brother after seeing the first plane hit, believing it was a small aircraft. His brother told him it was a passenger jet and described seeing people jumping from the neighboring tower. McGinley asked Danny if he was evacuating, and he said he'd been told to remain in place just before the South Tower was hit.

McGinley never spoke to him again.

"It is like the wound never healed, and every year we get salt poured back into that wound," McGinley said.

The families’ calls for answers extended beyond those killed on the day of the attacks. Relatives of first responders who later died from cancer and other illnesses linked to toxic exposure also gathered at the memorial to honor their loved ones.

Jen Nilsen, whose husband died in the attacks, said the pain remains as strong as ever 25 years later.

"It doesn’t change at the 25th year," Nilsen said. "The pain is still there."

Nilsen said she returns to the memorial because "this is where he is."

Her message to younger generations was simple.

"Never forget," she said. "Even though years go on, you never forget. You never get over it. The hurt is always there. The pain is always here."

item.title: Kansas renews Border War rivalry with Missouri by calling Tigers 'evil,' invoking slavery imagery
item.description: Kansas dropped a hype video calling Missouri evil over Civil War history ahead of Friday's Border Showdown, and critics say it went too far.
item.content:encoded:
You all know I'm a sucker for college football rivalries.

I even wrote about some of my favorite rivalries in the sport that are no longer annual contests, and one of the games that ended up on that list was Kansas vs. Missouri, so you can imagine my excitement when it was announced that these two foes would be going at it once more.

The Border War, as it was known until 2004, dates back to 1891 and features the kind of hatred and bad blood that makes college football rivalries hit differently than any other sport.

NOTRE DAME-USC RIVALRY GAME DISCUSSIONS BACK ON AFTER COLLEGE FOOTBALL SERIES ENDED IN 2026

That hatred was on full display thanks to a new hype video the Jayhawks dropped on social media earlier this week in anticipation for Friday's showdown, and, if we are being honest, they might have taken things just a bit too far.

Listen, I'm all for animus in college football rivalries but calling Mizzou evil because Missouri was a slave state 160 years ago feels a bit much, don't you think?

I love how they had to officially change the name from Border War to Border Showdown so as not to invoke images of armed conflict, but here comes the Kansas social media team saying, "Hey, remember the Civil War? Well, our opponent was on the side that wanted to keep using slaves."

That's painting with a bit of a broad brush, if you ask me.

Also, no one at the University of Missouri, be they students, faculty, or otherwise, were even alive at the time of the Civil War, so I'm not sure it's very polite or even correct to call them all "evil."

Most of the Mizzou players featured in Kansas's hype video are black, too, and I can assure you they didn't commit to the Tigers because they're pro slavery.

And the final cherry on top of this embarrassment sundae is that Metro Boomin, the producer for the song "Superhero (Heroes & Villains)" used in the video, is from, you guessed it, Missouri. (St. Louis.)

Well done all around, Jayhawks.

MINA KIMES THINKS PERCEPTION OF DIANNA RUSSINI-MIKE VRABEL SCANDAL IS UNFAIR TO WOMEN

Cunningham is real. She’s likable.

"You are kind of viewed as the leagues…ummm," Cowherd hesitated.

"Just say it," Cunningham interrupted.

"That is way better, I thought you were gonna go somewhere completely different," she joked.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Contrast Cunningham’s response with Angel Reese’s. Last month, Reese called herself "beautiful" multiple times and bragged that she looks good in a bikini. She then accused internet users of "sexualizing" her in the comments beneath those photos.

WNBA SILENCE ON DIJONAI CARRINGTON'S 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST EXPOSES SANDY BRONDELLO DOUBLE STANDARD

The DiJonai Carringtons and Jemele Hill types want to reduce Cunningham’s popularity down to her skin color. Of course they do. It’s their only card.

In reality, Cunningham is the type of woman Americans would embrace regardless of her skin color. She’s a smoking-hot badass who protects her teammates and trolls the media elite.
